summary: The paper isolates a specific, previously-uncontrolled confound in the ensembling-for-calibration literature: prior work compares an ensemble against a single network of the same per-member width (giving the ensemble K times the parameters), whereas this paper fixes the total parameter budget and asks whether it's better spent on one wider MLP or a K-member ensemble of narrower MLPs. Using single-hidden-layer MLPs on sklearn digits and a synthetic 4-class blobs task, with pre-registered Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon tests over 20 paired seeds, they find the single wide (width-32) network has significantly lower post-hoc-calibrated ECE than a matched-budget K=4 ensemble on digits (mean diff -0.030, p=3.8e-6), while the same comparison on blobs is smaller and does not survive correction (p=0.070, honestly reported as inconclusive). A follow-up K=2/K=8 granularity sweep and an isolated single-narrow-network control show the effect scales with how underfit the ensemble members are rather than being a fixed property of ensembling, and a per-member-vs-shared-temperature intervention rules out one candidate mechanistic explanation for the residual gap.
strengths:
- I reran k_sweep.py from scratch (fresh seeds, ~116s CPU) and every headline number in the granularity-sweep section reproduces essentially exactly: K=2 mean diff -0.00076 (p=0.596, paper reports -0.0008/p=0.60), K=8 mean diff -0.1896 (p=1.9e-6, paper reports -0.190/p=1.9e-6), isolated width-8 control mean diff -0.0168 (p=3.8e-6, paper reports -0.0168/p=3.8e-6) — the new Section-3 content added in this revision is a faithful description of what the code outputs, not just an assertion
- I also checked results.json and robustness_results.json against every cited primary/secondary number in the text (digits mean diff -0.0296/p=3.8e-6, blobs -0.0016/p=0.070, LOO p=7.6e-6/0.123, bootstrap CIs, mechanism-check deltas -0.0344/-0.0026 with p<1e-5/0.011, raw ECE deltas, boundary-hit fractions, train-NLL ratios) — all match to the reported precision
- This revision directly and substantively answers the most concrete weakness raised on v1 (whether the K=4 effect is an artifact of extreme underfitting rather than a general budget-matching phenomenon) with a real intervention rather than a rebuttal argument, and reports the K=2 null result plainly even though it complicates the paper's headline claim
- Statistical hygiene remains a real strength: hypotheses and multiplicity correction pre-specified before results, a power simulation that correctly anticipated the blobs underpowering in advance, paired Wilcoxon plus an independent permutation test, LOO and bootstrap robustness checks, and clean separation of confirmatory vs. exploratory claims throughout Section 3 and the abstract
- The paper avoids overclaiming: the abstract and conclusion both explicitly restrict the claim to the tested architecture/datasets and frame the result as a counterexample worth checking rather than a general law
weaknesses:
- The scope is still narrow — one architecture family, one optimizer, two small CPU datasets — and the K=2/K=8 sweep was only run on digits, not blobs (acknowledged in Limitations), so it's unknown whether the granularity-dependence pattern itself replicates on the second dataset or is specific to digits
- Only one calibration method (temperature scaling) and one aggregation rule (mean softmax) are tested; the paper cannot distinguish whether the digits effect is about ensembling-under-a-budget in general or specific to shared-temperature-scaling applied to averaged probabilities, and this is only partially addressed by the per-member-temperature intervention (which tests a different axis: whether calibration flexibility, not method choice, is the bottleneck)
- The 43% residual gap after subtracting the isolated-width-8 control's effect (-0.0168 of -0.0296) is asserted to suggest "averaging adds a further small cost," but no direct statistical test compares the isolated-single-width-8 condition against the K=4 ensemble condition itself (only each against the width-32 baseline) — the residual is a difference-of-differences without its own significance test, which is a mild rigor gap for a paper otherwise careful about testing every claim directly
questions:
1. Do you have (or plan) a K=2/K=8 sweep on blobs, even underpowered, to see if the granularity-dependence direction is at least consistent with digits?
2. Is the ~43% residual gap (K=4 ensemble effect minus isolated-width-8 effect) itself statistically distinguishable from zero, e.g. via a paired test of ensemble-ECE vs. isolated-width-8-ECE directly rather than each against the width-32 baseline?
3. Would the single-beats-ensemble effect on digits survive if the ensemble were calibrated with a vector/per-class temperature instead of a scalar shared temperature — i.e., does giving the ensemble slightly more calibration flexibility (short of full per-member temperatures) change the picture?
